He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being unreasonable in this situation with my dad and his business idea. Let me start by understanding the whole story. So, my dad came up with this business idea that I thought was genius. It was simple yet brilliant. But here's the thing: my dad is more of an introverted, quiet type. He's very intelligent, but he's never been good at getting things done. He's always had great ideas, but they never go anywhere because he doesn't take action. On the other hand, I'm more impulsive and headstrong, and while I'm not as intelligent as my dad, I do get things done. I'm more of a traditional masculine type, maybe fitting more into an older generation. When I heard my dad's idea, I was amazed, but I didn't think he could pull it off. So, I took the idea and ran with it. I got the IP rights and started the business two years ago. It's been a massive success, not making millions yet, but into the six figures, with the potential to make millions in the next half-decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but he didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom said I did her proud and did the right thing. I even confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels, and he called me a "fucking asshole," saying he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, "You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action." Then my sister walked in and started defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. Is AITA (Am I The Asshole) in this situation? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider a few things: 1. **Ownership of the Idea**: Did my dad own the idea, or was it something I could take and run with? Since I technically "stole" the idea, does that mean I took something that wasn't mine? 2. **My Dad's Ability to Act**: My dad has always been good at coming up with ideas but hasn't been able to execute them. Does that mean it's fair for me to take the idea and make it successful? 3. **Emotional Impact on My Dad**: My dad felt betrayed and was upset. How much weight should I give to his emotional response? 4. **My Offer to Share Profits**: I offered my dad 20% of the profits, but he rejected it. Does that mean he's being unreasonable, or is there another reason he might have refused? 5. **Family Dynamics**: My mom and granddad support me, but my sister supports my dad. How do these dynamics play into the situation? 6. **Ethical Considerations**: Is taking someone else's idea and profiting from it without their consent ethical? What are the boundaries here? 7. **Legal Aspects**: Did I get the IP rights legally, or was there something I missed in that process? 8. **Long-term Relationships**: How will this affect my relationship with my dad, sister, and other family members in the long run? 9. **Personal Growth and Reflection**: What have I learned from this situation, and how can I handle similar situations in the future? 10. **Alternative Solutions**: Is there a way to reconcile with my dad and find a middle ground that respects both our positions? Considering all these points, I need to weigh the pros and cons, understand the perspectives of all parties involved, and determine whether my actions were justified or if I'm being unreasonable. First, regarding ownership of the idea: If my dad came up with the idea, does he have a claim to it? In many cases, ideas are not protected unless they are patented or legally documented. Since I got the IP rights, it seems like I took legal steps to secure the idea, which might mean that legally, I own it now. However, ethically, taking an idea that someone else came up with and profiting from it without their consent could be seen as unfair. My dad might feel that I took something that was his, even if legally I have the rights. Next, considering my dad's inability to act: He's had ideas before but hasn't been able to execute them. Does that mean it's fair for me to take the idea and run with it? On one hand, I'm making use of the idea in a way my dad couldn't, which could be seen as a positive. On the other hand, it's still his idea, and I'm profiting from it without his involvement. Emotionally, my dad felt betrayed. Betrayal is a strong emotion, and it's important to acknowledge that. Even if I believe I did the right thing, causing my dad to feel this way is significant. It's worth considering whether there's a way to mend this relationship or at least understand his perspective better. My offer to share profits was rejected. This could mean several things. Maybe my dad feels that 20% is not enough, or perhaps he doesn't want to be associated with the business anymore. It could also be that he's hurt and not ready to accept the offer, even if it's fair. Family dynamics are also at play here. My mom and granddad support me, which is helpful, but my sister supports my dad. This could create tension within the family. It's important to maintain harmony, so finding a way to resolve this conflict is crucial. Ethically, taking someone else's idea and profiting from it without their consent is a gray area. There's a balance between respecting someone's intellectual property and recognizing that ideas need action to become successful. It's possible that my dad feels that I disrespected him by taking his idea, while I might feel that I'm the one who made it a reality. Legally, since I secured the IP rights, I might be in the clear. However, it's important to ensure that I didn't overlook any legal steps or that my dad didn't have prior claims to the idea that I didn't consider. Looking at the long-term relationships, this situation could have lasting effects on my family ties. It's worth considering whether the success of the business is worth the potential strain on these relationships. In terms of personal growth, this situation offers an opportunity to reflect on how I handle conflicts, respect others' contributions, and balance my own ambitions with family relationships. Alternative solutions could involve finding a way to involve my dad in the business, even if it's in a limited capacity, or finding another way to compensate him for the idea beyond just profit-sharing. It might also involve having an open and honest conversation to understand each other's perspectives better. Overall, while I might feel that I did the right thing by taking the idea and making it successful, it's clear that my dad feels hurt and betrayed. It's important to acknowledge his feelings and find a way to reconcile our differences, even if it means making some compromises.
